content.summary_of_the_paper: In this paper, the authors propose an ordinal regression algorithm with the following features. First, the algorithm guarantees unimodal output probabilities, which is an attractive feature in many applications. Second, the model is trained using optimal transport loss instead of the commonly-used maximum likelihood. Last, the authors claim that the algorithm achieves the so-called uncertainty awareness in the sense that the model is more confident about correct predictions, compared to incorrect ones.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
The authors claim that existing approaches of obtaining unimodal output distribution are oftentimes not enforced. However, this claim is incorrect and the literature review is not inadequate. For example, a so-called unimodal-concentrated loss (UCL)-based method was proposed by [https://arxiv.org/pdf/2204.00309.pdf] and ensures the unimodality of the learned distribution. Moreover, this UCL paper further claims that the concentrated loss maximizes the probability at the ground-truth in a fully adaptive way for individual instances. 

The discussion of "uncertainty awareness" is vague and superficial. While it is true to argue that "the confidence in the prediction should be greater in cases of correct predictions, comparing to incorrect ones," the authors abruptly define a regularization term in Eq. (7) without providing any in-depth discussion about how to achieve uncertainty awareness with what type of techniques.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: Novelty/contribution is limited and some claims are not well backed up.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper introduces a technique for performing ordinal regression that overcomes multiple weaknesses of prior approaches: (1) unlike other work, it is guaranteed by construction to produce unimodal output probabilities, (2) the loss function treats "near-miss" prediction errors as less bad than larger errors, unlike other work where the loss function only cares about the probability assigned to the correct class, and (3) it introduces a regularization term that penalizes the model when its incorrect predictions have lower average entropy than its correct predictions.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
* Achieves unimodality in a straightforward way, although it seems like it may be a bit unnecessarily restrictive: the output probabilities are equally-spaced integrals over a Gaussian density function. This gives 2 degrees of freedom (mean and variance of the Gaussian), but that may not be enough expressiveness for some problems with a large number of classes.
* The loss function is a clear improvement over simple cross entropy, which completely ignores class ordering, a central component of ordinal regression.
Weaknesses:
* I don't understand the purpose of the regularizer that penalizes the model when its incorrect predictions have lower entropy than its correct predictions. This doesn't seem to have any qualitative effect beyond the (un-regularized) loss function, which already encourages the model to put as much probability mass as possible onto its correct predictions, while spreading the mass across multiple classes for incorrect predictions. Does this actually improve performance? If so, why?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
* The paper is very clearly written and easy to understand. I would have no problem implementing these ideas myself after just reading the paper.
* The paper doesn't seem very original to me, as it is applying multiple pre-existing ideas to the task of ordinal regression. None of the individual ideas described here strike me as surprising or clever, with the exception of having the model output both the mean and variance of the predictive distribution. I'm not very familiar with the state of the art in ordinal regression, but I'm surprised, for example, that the proportional odds model as described here would be the dominant approach when it has such obvious drawbacks that can be easily overcome.
content.summary_of_the_review: I'm not sure that it meets the bar for novelty and significance. The approach seems like a somewhat straightforward application of existing ideas to an existing problem. I'm a bit surprised that the state of the art for ordinal regression seems to have the glaring problems that this paper overcomes relatively easily.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper proposes an algorithm that enforces unimodality, and learns to output
the unimodal distribution with an optimal transport loss that is regularized
through a hinge-like entropy term. The reasoning for the optimal transport loss
is to consider all probability mass, which the likelihood does not, and the
regularizer is for "uncertainty awareness The proposed algorithm is benchmarked
against 4 deep ordinal regression baselines and on 8 datasets. The empirical
evidence suggests that the proposed algorithm is competitive with the baselines.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths
---------

-   The proposed algorithm seems to meet the goals that it set out to
    achieve, namely it provides a unimodal ordinal regression method
    that is learned not with likelihood but optimal transport.
-   The paper is overall easy to understand, and I found Figures 1-4
    greatly help in understanding the role of optimal transport in the
    ordinal regression problem.

Weaknesses
----------

-   Several statements in the paper are very unclear and would benefit
    from additional evidence through either experiments, references or
    examples. Please see the "Detailed Comments" of this review for
    particular examples.
-   While it easy to understand the individual components of the
    proposed algorithm, each of which have some representation in
    ordinal regression, the overall motivation for the proposed
    algorithm is unconvincing. The role of the regularizer, for example,
    is vague in its effect on the solution theoretically (little
    argument or discussion) and empirically (no ablation). Uncertainty
    awareness is not really defined or tested empirically, and seems
    redundant with the argument for optimal transport. The need for
    enforcing unimodality is also not clearly demonstrated, but seems to
    be a relevant research topic in some respect.
-   The experiments, while covering relevant baselines and many
    datasets, fail to convince. They demonstrate that the proposed
    method is competitive with, but not superior to, the baselines. This
    alone is okay, but there is no further depth to the experimental
    study. It is not clear, for example, whether the proposed algorithm
    benefits most from (1) enforcing unimodality, (2) the optimal
    transport loss or (3) the regularizer. The paper would benefit from
    an ablation study and a deeper analysis at the role of the proposed
    regularizer and the interpretation behind the proposed entropy ratio
    metric.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Detailed Comments (Clarity, Quality, Novetly, Reproducibility)
--------------------------------------------------------------

-   Section 1, Paragraph 2: "Hence one may expect that typical ordinal
    regression algorithms have potential to outperform classification or
    regression approaches"

    It would be good to provide references or evidence for this
    particular claim, as the experiments in this paper do not
    demonstrate this. While it may be obvious that treating the problem
    "faithfully" as ordinal regression is a good idea, I only found
    evidence of this in checking the papers for the baselines. I am
    unable to say whether this holds true for your experiments because
    thee results reported in the submission differ from the baseline
    papers (e.g. Diaz \\& Marathe (2019) results on Adience differ from
    what you report, possibly due to implementation differences.)

-   Section 1, Paragraph 3: "We argue that likelihood is a sub-optimal
    measure of quality for ordinal regression setup, as it only
    considers the probability mass the model assigns to the true class,
    ignoring the remaining mass."

    This is true of likelihood estimation, as you demonstrate in the
    submission. But, I don't think likelihood's estimation inability to
    consider probability off the true class is enough to suggest that
    you need to do away with likelihood entirely and move to optimal
    transport For example, the entropy regularizer you suggest in
    combination with likelihood estimation would allow for probability
    mass to be considered off the correct class.

-   Section 1, Paragraph 4: "Although there are domains in which
    unimodality is not necessarily a desirable property, (…) in many
    other real world domains it is a natural requirement,"

    It is hard to argue that unimodality of model outputs is a
    requirement. Rather, it is a useful inductive bias if a domain
    expert deems it a relevant modelling assumption. Even with this
    assumption in place, it is not necessarily obvious that a
    unimodality assumption necessarily improves the modelling
    predictions. The results in Table 1, the baseline by Liu et al.
    2019a, has the lowest unimodality score but has intersecting
    confidence intervals in all reported benchmarks.

-   Section 2, Paragraph 1: "We argue that the multi-label approach has
    two major problematic aspects: first, the output probabilities are
    not always guaranteed to be consistent, in the sense of increasing
    cumulative distribution (i.e., we would like to predict Pr(y ≤ 1) ≤
    Pr(y ≤ 2) ≤ . . . ≤ Pr(y ≤ k)."

    This is not entirely obvious to me, perhaps a reference or example
    would help illustrate this point. If the output is a distribution,
    as is the case with multi-label classification with softmax or some
    other normalization, then it does define a valid cumulative
    distribution.

-   Section 2, Paragraph 2: It is true that limiting to the Poisson
    distribution alone does not allow one to control the relative
    dispersion and the mode of the distribution independently. The paper
    by Beckham \\& Pal (2017) addresses this by adding $\tau$ which
    encodes uncertainty ($\tau \rightarrow \infty$ tends to uniformity
    and $\tau \rightarrow 0$ tends to one-hot). Hence, it is not limited
    to a single parameter and $\tau$ seems to address the limitation
    that you point out in this work. While this can treated as a
    hyperparameter, it can also be learned (both are done in the paper).

-   Section 3.2: Presumably, the optimal transport loss is used because
    the likelihood loss doesn't consider the probability mass off the
    true class. This point is not really well demonstrated in this
    section, nor in the subsequent sections nor the experiments.

-   Section 4, Equation 7: The precise formula of the entropy term is
    not entirely clear, nor is the intuitive meaning.

    The first problem is that the definition used for the entropy is not
    included, nor is the precise definition of $p_\theta(x)$. I assume
    that $p_\theta(x)$ is the discrete distribution induced by $p_i(x)$,
    where dependence on $theta$ is implicit and that
    $p_\theta(x) = [p_1(x),\dotso,p_k(x)]$. Then the entropy term is the
    usual discrete (non-differential) entropy:
    $H(p_\theta(x)) = \sum_i p_i(x) \log
       p_i(x)$.

    But even with this, it is not entirely clear why we would want the
    average entropy over incorrect predictions to be higher than the
    average entropy over correct predictions. Nor is the contribution of
    this regularizer ablated with respect to wasserstein loss or even
    with the likelihood loss.

-   Section 5.2: " We performed 5 independent trials, using the same
    train-validation-test splits for all methods."

    Given that many of the results have overlapping confidence
    intervals, the experiments would benefit from a much larger number
    of runs.

-   Table 1: It is not clear the method used for identifying the best
    performing model (I assume the bold face indicates the
    top-performer). For one, the confidence intervals reported are often
    intersecting with the baseline. Several metrics are reported, but
    very little is spent explaining the results. It would be interesting
    to see how the entropy ratio can be interpreted or even why certain
    top-performing algorithms differ with respect to different metrics.

Minor Comments
--------------

-   Section 5.2, baselines: The choice of baselines seem comprehensive,
    but it would be better to describe the baselines in of the three
    criteria you outline: (1) unimodality, (2) uncertainty and (3)
    optimal transport vs MLE. This information is somewhat present in
    the current outline of the baselines, but the other details are
    distracting and not relevant (and are already discussed in the
    related works)
content.summary_of_the_review:
The proposed algorithm is an interesting combination of ideas.
Unfortunately, the paper does not clearly demonstrate the strength of
this combination nor does it thoroughly validate the individual choices.
Thereform, I am leaning towards rejection.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper introduces a new approach for ordinal regression that improves on the proportional odds model (POM) in that i) model probability distributions are always unimodal (i.e. predictive probabilities increase up to a certain label and decrease thereafter), and ii) the loss function used in the new approach penalizes the lack of concentration of the predictive distribution around its mode, whereas the cross-entropy loss utilized by POM only penalizes the difference between the predictive mode and the true label.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
- **Strength**: Unimodality can indeed be a desirable property of an ordinal regression model, as well illustrated by the cancer tumor example in the paper. The proposed approach is a satisfactory solution.  

- **Weaknesses**: The need for concentration around the predictive mode isn't as well argued in the paper. Neither is the fact that this concentration is intrinsically related to awareness of prediction uncertainty, a suggestion that appears throughout the paper. This is certainly not true of epistemic uncertainty.

Consider for instance the case where $x$ is independent from $y$. The best model cannot do better than positing that all labels are equally probable. In other words, there is no epistemic uncertainty left despite the predictive model being flat.

On a related note, the paper is missing asymptotics on the effect of the regularizer on the solution (e.g. bias, consistency, etc.). The extension from POM is simple enough that the paper could benefit greatly from such analyses.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper is clear, well-written, although the extension from POM is rather straightforward and the paper could contain more implementation details.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper is interesting, reads well, but the case for the regularizer and its effect on the solution should be clarified.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes ordinal logistic regression, addressing the problem of the popular used proportional odds model. The proposed algorithm does not make ties in the class probability, and two hyperparameters provide flexible modeling. Experiments were conducted to show the superiority of the proposed algorithm. The key of the proposed algorithm is to use the normal distribution for the prediction of probability and put a regularizer term to assess the uncertainty.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Pros: 
The ordinal logistic regression can be a model to make the machine learning area more plenty. The use of normal distribution and earth move distance is interesting. The proposed algorithm is aligned with machine learning and AI algorithms. Experiments are interesting in the accuracy measures and entropy ratio.     

Cons:
The authors consider only the logistic distribution in the conventional ordinal logistic regression. However, as known, there are many random variables for the modeling. In the view of link, probit, complementary log-log link, etc. exist in the ordinal logistic regression. The study for these links was not done or written in the paper. In addition, the authors consider only image datasets. However, many structured datasets are applied in the ordinal logistic regression.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity: 
The motivation and algorithm are clear, and the use of earth move has not the obvious motivations. Experiments results show that the unimodal ratios are almost the same in many algorithms except for some algorithm and dataset combinations. In contrast, the entropy ratio is consistently large. I doubt that unimodality is the main property of the proposed algorithm, and unimodality is important. In addition, at least for me, it is not obvious what’s the main difference compared to baseline algorithms.    

Quality:
Well-written. The organization is somewhat rough. The introduction of each component of the algorithm lacks detailed explanations or motivations. Experimental results support the authors’ algorithms. However, I feel that a more thorough review of ordinal logistic regression can make this paper strong. 

Novelty & reproducibility
The novelty is incremental. The proposed algorithm uses the standard algorithms, therefore it seems that there are no severe problems with the reproducibility

content.title: A Unimodal, Uncertainty-Aware Deep Learning Approach for Ordinal Regression
content.abstract:
Ordinal regression is an important area in machine learning, and many algorithms were proposed to approach it. In this work, we propose an ordinal regression prediction algorithm, based on deep learning machinery and inspired by the well-known Proportional Odds model. Our proposed approach has three key components: first, it is designed to guarantee unimodal output probabilities, which is a desired element in many real world applications. Second, we argue that the standard maximum likelihood is sub-optimal for ordinal regression problems and train our model using optimal transport loss, as it naturally captures the order of the classes. Third, we design a novel regularizer aiming to make the model uncertainty-aware, in the sense of making the model more confident about correct predictions, comparing to wrong predictions. In addition, we propose a novel uncertainty-awareness evaluation measure. Experimental results on eight real-world datasets
demonstrate that our proposed approach consistently performs on par with and often better than several recently proposed deep learning approaches for ordinal regression, in terms of both accuracy and uncertainty-awareness, while having a guarantee on the output unimodality.
